text: In 1925, a man with a forged letter sold the Eiffel Tower.
It was not his. He sold it anyway.
Then he tried to sell it again.
I'm Sir Digsworth, and this is the story of Victor Lustig.
Lustig is born in 1890, in a small town in Bohemia. On his first day of school, he is expelled for being rude to the teacher.
A later school report calls him an idiot.
He is not an idiot. At boarding school he learns English, French, Italian and Hungarian.
He starts on the ocean liners between France and New York, posing as a producer who needs investors for a Broadway show. There is no show.
Then comes the money box: a mahogany box that, he says, can copy any banknote. It only needs six hours.
He puts in a note. Six hours later, out comes a second one. It is real, because he hid it in there earlier.
Then he sells the box, for thousands of dollars.
One buyer is a Texas sheriff, who chases him all the way to Chicago. Lustig pays him back. In fake money.
In 1925 he is in Paris, reading the newspaper. The Eiffel Tower, it says, is getting too expensive to maintain and repaint.
So Lustig has some government paper forged, and becomes the Deputy Director-General of the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs.
He invites a small group of scrap metal dealers to an expensive hotel, and tells them a secret. The government wishes to sell the tower for scrap.
One dealer, André Poisson, badly wants to be an important man. He pays a large bribe, and then he pays for the tower: about 70,000 francs in all.
Lustig flees to Austria and reads the newspapers. Nothing. Poisson is too ashamed to tell the police.
So, later that year, he goes back to Paris and tries to sell the tower again. This time somebody tells the police, and Lustig sails for America.
There he asks the gangster Al Capone to invest 50,000 dollars. He keeps the money in a safe for two months, then gives it all back, and says the deal fell through.
Then he says he is broke. And Capone gives him 5,000 dollars to tide him over.
In the 1930s he turns to printing money. With a chemist and a pharmacist, he makes thousands of fake dollars a month, for five years.
It ends when he is unfaithful to his girlfriend, Billy May. She telephones the federal agents.
He is arrested in New York in May 1935. He has a key he will not explain. It opens a locker at Times Square station, with 51,000 fake dollars and the printing plates inside.
The day before his trial, he pretends to be ill, and climbs out of the jail on a rope. He is free for 27 days.
Then he is caught in Pittsburgh, and sent to Alcatraz for 20 years.
Victor Lustig died in 1947. His death certificate gives his occupation as apprentice salesman. And counterfeiter.
The Eiffel Tower is still not for sale.
I'm Sir Digsworth. Do mind your wallet.
